actions.findings:
Objective physical records emerge through the environmental encoding of system pointer states, which function as redundant broadcast structures. [peer-feb7891b837e677ec8e3c811] [source-0af46fdac3ca4296]

The thermodynamic cost of information erasure provides a fundamental stability bound for physical records. [peer-3d80ce4af7c184d54bcc9333]
actions.limitations: The current findings rely on theoretical frameworks, including SBS and generalized quantum Darwinism, which often assume idealized Markovian environmental couplings. Real-world implementation remains constrained by finite-size effects and non-Markovian noise, which have not been fully mapped against the specific robustness thresholds identified.
actions.next_questions: How do non-Markovian memory effects in the environment influence the resilience of Spectrum Broadcast Structures? Can Landauer-limited erasure rates be experimentally correlated with the decay of redundant pointer states in open quantum systems?
actions.reason: Notebook revision required to integrate thermodynamic constraints on record stability with existing redundancy frameworks.
actions.summary: Robustness in physical records is achieved when system pointer states are redundantly encoded into environmental degrees of freedom, enabling independent observers to reach consensus. This process, formalizable through Spectrum Broadcast Structures (SBS) and quantum Darwinism, effectively 'broadcasts' information. Furthermore, thermodynamic constraints, specifically the energy cost of erasing information (Landauer's principle), bound the long-term stability of these records in both classical and quantum substrates.
actions.title: Robustness and Redundancy in Quantum and Classical Records

proposal.summary: Revised operational analysis of physical record robustness, clarifying the roles of environmental redundancy and thermodynamic stability.
